newsitem.title: MEXICO: Analysts warm to Televisa 1997 advertising revenues.
newsitem.headline: Analysts warm to Televisa 1997 advertising revenues.

text.p: Mexico's Grupo Televisa will enjoy a windfall in new advertising next year after two years of unusually slim ad revenues for the media giant, analysts said on Tuesday.
Televisa reported this week that up-front ad sales for 1997 grew about 9.5 percent in real terms compared to this year, slightly higher than expected by most industry analysts.

The company's French Plan, an advertising scheme that charges clients ahead of time for most of next year's ads, garnered 5.685 billion pesos as of mid-November's closing date compared to 4.024 billion during the same period of 1995.

"With anticipated higher 1997 revenue reflecting the 9.5 percent French Plan advance and higher real (ad) rates...we expect Televisa's turnaround to gain strength in 1997," Salomon Brothers analyst Marla Marron said in a report.
Other analysts the French Plan could be a liability ahead, and said the media firm's longer-term picture remains fuzzy due to competition from rivals such as upstart TV Azteca.
Most of the gains in ad revenue was due to growth in the Mexican advertising market as a whole, and not to Televisa's efforts to coax more money from existing customers.

New advertisers, especially telecommunications companies that will compete with current monopoly Telmex beginning next year and banks that plan to offer private pension funds starting next July, accounted for just under $500 million of the plan's revenues, analysts said.
That growth could be more of a one-time event than a signal of a continued boom in advertising, analysts said.

"It turns out that Televisa's traditional French Plan clients have increased their advertising spending by barely 2.1 percent (in real terms) in 1997 compared to 1996," wrote Francisco Rivero, an analyst at Valores Finamex in New York.
There are two likely explanations as to why Televisa's regular clients increased their advertising by so little.

Some advertisers may feel the economy is not yet on solid enough footing to justify new advertising. Many of those are likely to come in next year through additional advertising, called "top-off", if the economy picks up, analysts said.

The other, more ominous, explanation is that Televisa is losing clients to rival TV Azteca and cable company Multivision. Azteca now has at least 25 percent of TV ratings, although its percentage of total ad revenue still lags at about 18 percent.
"In these numbers, you can see a slight erosion of market share to Azteca," said Alexander Rishawi, an analyst at D.A. Campbell in Los Angeles.
Televisa's loss of the Unilever account a few months ago sent a signal to other advertisers that Televisa was no longer the only game in town, Rishawi said.
"For the advertiser in Mexico today, there are a lot more options than there were three or four years ago," he said.
Televisa has acknowledged that Azteca's competition has cost it market share and said that it will use its dominant position in the market to defend itself.

Industry analysts believe Televisa was more flexible this time around in offering its French Plan. Reforma newspaper columnist Alberto Aguilar said the company offered PepsiCo 10 free ad spots for each paid spot in order to ensure it obtained the contract.

The pay-ahead French plan may also not help in an increasingly competitive market, analysts said. Televisa implemented the plan years ago when it had a near total lock on the TV-viewing audience, and today it is the only media company in Mexico to bill that way.
Discounts or not, Televisa still does hold a dominant share of the market and can largely dictate the terms of advertising to its clients.

"The French Plan still shows Televisa's muscle. If you have 75 percent of the ad market, no big consumer products maker can pass you up," said Shayne McGuire, an analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Mexico City.
